newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FORECAST - Brazil April trade gap seen at $750 mln.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Brazil April trade gap seen at $750 mln.

text.p: Brazil should post a $750 million trade gap in April, the first monthly trade deficit this year to dip below $1.0 billion, but not a very encouraging number, economists said.
"Due to seasonal factors we should expect a lower trade deficit in April, but this is not low enough," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC bank in Brazil.
"If we want to keep the trade deficit at $10 billion to $12 billion this year, then this is not a very enthusiastic result," he said.

The Commerce Ministry on Tuesday said the trade deficit through the first four weeks of April totaled $621 million. Trade figures for the entire month were expected later this week or early next week.

Forecasts of a $700 million to $800 million deficit in April are considerably bettter than the average $1.0 billion monthly trade gaps Brazil saw in the first quarter. But economists say they are not cheered by the figures.

Brazil's export season is in full swing from April to June, when exports of soy and other crops reach their peak. Normally, the country's trade accounts are in equilibrium or slight deficit at this time of the year.
But persistent import growth has forced economists to rachet up their monthly second quarter deficit forecasts from the $200-$300 million range to $700-$800 million.

"The daily average for imports so far in April is about $260 million. Normally it's about $240 million so this worries me. I think importers are anticipating new import restrictons next month so they are bringing in more goods now to beat the measures," said Roberto Padovani, an economist at the consulting firm Trend Analise in Sao Paulo.
After stiffening import financing rules last month, the government is now widely expected to add credit curbs for the purchase of cars and electronic goods sometime in May.

The trade gap is Brazil's chief short-term concern because it is one of the leading pressures on the nation's bulging current account balance of payments deficit, which is expected to surpass $30 billion this year.
Average monthly trade deficits of about $700 million from April to June will take Brazil's second quarter trade gap to about $2.0 billion, on top of a first quarter gap of $3.06 billion.
Even more worrying is the fact that average monthly deficits in the third and fourth quarters are expected to be well above $1.0 billion.
"We will wind up with an $11 billion trade gap in 1997 if the government imposes some new measures. If not, the deficit will be above $13 billion," Padovani said.

Still, the government was seen having no problem financing the current account gap through short-term capital flows, international bond issues and foreign direct investment, such as the planned privatization of state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, which is seen bringing in some $5.0 billion to government coffers.
